# Fixing soggy garden soil

A bed that stays waterlogged suffocates roots: soil pores fill with water instead of air, roots cannot respire, and they rot even though the plants look thirsty above ground. Symptoms mimic drought stress — wilting and yellowing leaves — so push a finger into the soil before assuming more water is needed. Soggy ground also invites fungal root diseases that a well-drained bed resists.

Adding coarse sand to clay rarely helps; at moderate amounts it packs into a denser matrix, like making mortar. The reliable fixes are organic matter and geometry. Work in finished compost and aged leaf mold over seasons to open the clay's structure, and let earthworms maintain the channels. Where a season of amendment cannot wait, build a raised bed fifteen to twenty centimeters high filled with bought loam and compost, lifting roots above the water table entirely.

A French drain is the option when runoff ponds after rain: a gravel-filled trench sloping downhill carries water away from the bed to a discharge point. Check for the compaction layer first — a hardpan from digging or traffic traps water at its surface no matter how loose the soil above it. Break it with a fork before deciding the drainage is hopeless. Avoid working wet clay; every footprint and shovel slice seals it further.
